steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: What’s ___ like? / He’s the kind of person who ___. / We get along well. Table (누구 → 어떤 사람 (the kind of person who …)):
- my team leader 팀장님 → …who listens to everyone.
- my best friend 친한 친구 → …who always makes me laugh.
- my neighbor 이웃 → …who helps everyone.
- my coworker 동료 → …who never gives up.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
She’s the kind of person *who* plans everything. 
여기서 who가 주어예요. *동사*는 그 사람에 맞춰요: who *plans* / who always *helps*(she라서 -s) 
a friend *who* makes me laugh 나를 웃게 하는 친구

What’s Chloe *like*? → She’s really outgoing. 
What does she look like? 생김새 · What does she like? 좋아하는 것
errors: She’s like a sister to me.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- who 절 — ~하는 사람: She’s the kind of person who plans everything. / 여기서 who가 주어예요. 동사는 그 사람에 맞춰요: who plans / who always helps(she라서 -s) / a friend who makes me laugh 나를 웃게 하는 친구
- What’s ~ like? — 어떤 사람이에요?: What’s Chloe like? → She’s really outgoing. / What does she look like? 생김새 · What does she like? 좋아하는 것
Common mistakes on screen:
- What’s she like it? → What’s she like? (like로 끝나요(it 없이).)
- She’s someone who plan ahead. → She’s someone who plans ahead. (who가 she를 가리켜서 plans.)
- We get along good. → We get along well. (‘사이좋게’는 well.)
- She’s like sister to me. → She’s like a sister to me. (sister 앞에 a.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: who 절 — ~하는 사람: She’s the kind of person who plans everything. 여기서 who가 주어예요. 동사는 그 사람에 맞춰요: who plans / who always helps(she라서 -s) a friend who makes me laugh 나를 웃게 하는 친구
What’s ~ like? — 어떤 사람이에요?: What’s Chloe like? → She’s really outgoing. What does she look like? 생김새 · What does she like? 좋아하는 것

She’s someone who plan ahead. → She’s someone who plans ahead.
We get along good. → We get along well.
She’s like sister to me. → She’s like a sister to me.

steps.note: 예) Chloe / makes everyone laugh → A: What’s Chloe like? B: She’s the kind of person who makes everyone laugh.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) Chloe / makes everyone laugh → A: What’s Chloe like? B: She’s the kind of person who makes everyone laugh. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: Chloe → makes everyone laugh | my team leader → listens to everyone | my neighbor → helps everyone | my friend → never gives up.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: He’s the kind of person who ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "What’s she like?" (어떤 사람이에요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What’s ___ like?" / "He’s the kind of person who ___." / "We get along well.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 성격 말하기: "She’s really easygoing." (정말 편하고 느긋한 사람이에요., 보통); "He can be a bit stubborn." (좀 고집이 셀 때가 있어요., 보통); "He’s got a great sense of humor." (유머 감각이 대단해요., 친근); "She’s someone you can trust." (믿을 수 있는 사람이에요., 보통)
- 사이 말하기: "We have a lot in common." (공통점이 많아요., 보통); "We don’t always see eye to eye." (늘 생각이 같지는 않아요., 보통); "We’ve known each other for years." (서로 안 지 오래됐어요., 보통)
- 마음 표현하기: "I look up to her." (그녀를 존경해요. 본받고 싶어요., 보통); "She’s like a sister to me." (제게 언니(누나) 같은 사람이에요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 좋은 점 · 부드럽게 말하기

*reliable* 믿음직한 · *generous* 너그러운 · *patient* 참을성 있는

그 자리에 없는 사람 이야기는 성격만, 좋은 점 위주로 해요(외모 평가·험담 ×).
함께 일하는 사람

*colleague* 동료 · *fellow* designers 동료 디자이너들 
*leader* 이끄는 사람 · *partner* 짝, 파트너 
We work *closely* together. 긴밀하게 함께 일해요. 
I *have faith in* her. 그녀를 믿어요.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:

- 함께 일하는 사람: colleague 동료 · fellow designers 동료 디자이너들 / leader 이끄는 사람 · partner 짝, 파트너 / We work closely together. 긴밀하게 함께 일해요. / I have faith in her. 그녀를 믿어요.

Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.

items: We have a lot in common.
He handles problems in a mature way.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: personality (성격) — "She has a warm personality."; character (성격, 됨됨이) — "He has a calm character."; honest (정직한, 솔직한) — "She’s always honest with me."; common (공통의(have ~ in common)) — "We have a lot in common."; relationship (관계, 사이) — "We have a good relationship."; respect (존중하다; 존경) — "I really respect him."; admire (감탄하다, 존경하다) — "I admire her honesty."; mature (성숙한, 어른스러운) — "He handles problems in a mature way."; description (설명, 묘사) — "Read the job description."; strongly (강하게, 굳게) — "I strongly believe it.".

items: She’s really ___. / He’s the kind of person who ___.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What’s your best friend like?" (hint on screen: She’s really ___. / He’s the kind of person who ___.)
- "Who do you get along well with? Why?" (hint on screen: I get along well with my ___. We have a lot in common.)
- "What kind of person is a good leader?" (hint on screen: A good leader is someone who ___.)
- "Is there someone you look up to?" (hint on screen: Yes, I look up to my ___. She’s the kind of person who ___.)
- "Ask me what someone is like." (hint on screen: What’s your ___ like?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: The Job Description
steps.text: That evening, Jiwoo read the job description again. One line said, “We want someone who enjoys teamwork.” Jiwoo smiled. Her team leader now is a calm, mature person. He’s never aggressive in meetings, and he *breaks up* big projects into small steps. Last year, he *got rid of* long Friday meetings, and everyone loved it. And Chloe’s best characteristic is her honesty. Jiwoo really admires that. The new job sounded attractive, but she strongly felt her fellow designers here were special, too. Then Daniel sent a message: “I have faith in you. Good luck!”
steps.gloss: aggressive 공격적인 · break up 나누다 · get rid of 없애다 · characteristic 특징 · attractive 매력적인 · fellow 같은 처지의, 동료의 · faith 믿음

What does Jiwoo admire?

steps.title: 가장 기억에 남는 일
steps.title_en: What was the most memorable moment?
steps.goal: 가장 기억에 남는 일을 묻고, 이유와 함께 말하고, ‘처음’이었던 경험 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 2월 말 오후, 회사 탕비실. 클로이가 휴대폰 화면(호숫가 사진, 글자 없이)을 지우에게 내밀고, 지우가 머그잔을 든 채 반가운 얼굴로 들여다봄. 창밖은 맑은 겨울 하늘(글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "What was the most memorable moment?" (가장 기억에 남는 일). Goal: 가장 기억에 남는 일을 묻고, 이유와 함께 말하고, ‘처음’이었던 경험 말하기. Today's scene: 2월 말 오후, 회사 탕비실. 클로이가 휴대폰 화면(호숫가 사진, 글자 없이)을 지우에게 내밀고, 지우가 머그잔을 든 채 반가운 얼굴로 들여다봄. 창밖은 맑은 겨울 하늘(글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "What was the most memorable ___?".

steps.when: 가장 기억에 남는 일을 물어요. 긴 형용사는 *the most* + 형용사.
steps.extra: What was the most memorable trip of your life?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "What was the most memorable ___?" (가장 기억에 남는 ~는 뭐였어요?). When to use it: 가장 기억에 남는 일을 물어요. 긴 형용사는 the most + 형용사. Note: What was the most memorable trip of your life?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "My most memorable ___ was ___ because ___.".

steps.when: 무엇이었는지와 이유를 같이 말해요. my가 있으면 the 없이.
steps.extra: My most memorable trip was my trip to Toronto because I saw the lake.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "My most memorable ___ was ___ because ___." (가장 기억에 남는 ~는 …였어요, 왜냐하면 ~.). When to use it: 무엇이었는지와 이유를 같이 말해요. my가 있으면 the 없이. Note: My most memorable trip was my trip to Toronto because I saw the lake.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "It was the first time I’d ever ___.".

steps.en: It was the first time I’d ever ___.
steps.when: ‘태어나서 처음’을 말해요. I’d = I had, 뒤에 *p.p.*. 통째로 익혀요.
steps.extra: It was the first time I’d ever been abroad.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "It was the first time I’d ever ___." (그때 처음으로 ~해 봤어요.). When to use it: ‘태어나서 처음’을 말해요. I’d = I had, 뒤에 p.p.. 통째로 익혀요. Note: It was the first time I’d ever been abroad.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Memories · 2월 말 오후, 회사 탕비실에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Memories · 2월 말 오후, 회사 탕비실에서

lines.en: Ooh, look! My phone just showed me this photo. Toronto, last spring!
lines.ko: 와, 이거 봐요! 휴대폰에 이 사진이 떴어요. 작년 봄 토론토!

lines.en: Wow! I remember it like it was yesterday. That was my best trip ever.
lines.ko: 와! 어제 일처럼 기억나요. 제 최고의 여행이었어요.

lines.en: Really? {{What was the most memorable}} moment?
lines.ko: 정말요? 가장 기억에 남는 순간은 뭐였어요?

lines.en: The first morning at the lake. {{It was the first time I’d ever}} been abroad. I had never seen anything like it.
lines.ko: 호숫가에서의 첫 아침이요. 처음으로 해외에 가 본 거였어요. 그런 건 처음 봤어요.

lines.en: Aww. So what made it so special?
lines.ko: 아이, 좋다. 그럼 뭐가 그렇게 특별했어요?

lines.en: The lake was enormous, and your family was so kind. It was a once-in-a-lifetime experience.
lines.ko: 호수가 어마어마하게 컸고, 클로이 가족이 정말 친절했어요. 평생 한 번 있을 경험이었어요.

lines.en: Once-in-a-lifetime! That sounded so natural!
lines.ko: ‘평생 한 번’! 정말 자연스러웠어요!

lines.en: Thanks! What about you? What was your most memorable project?
lines.ko: 고마워요! 클로이는요? 가장 기억에 남는 작업은 뭐였어요?

lines.en: {{My most memorable}} project {{was}} my first video {{because}} I made it all by myself. I put my heart and soul into it.
lines.ko: 제일 기억에 남는 작업은 첫 영상이에요, 혼자서 다 만들었거든요. 온 마음을 다 쏟았어요.

lines.en: That sounds unforgettable.
lines.ko: 잊지 못할 일이었겠네요.

lines.en: It was. Looking back, it changed my life. It still makes me smile.
lines.ko: 그랬죠. 돌이켜 보면 그게 제 인생을 바꿨어요. 지금도 웃음이 나요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Memories · 2월 말 오후, 회사 탕비실에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Chloe: "Ooh, look! My phone just showed me this photo. Toronto, last spring!" (와, 이거 봐요! 휴대폰에 이 사진이 떴어요. 작년 봄 토론토!)
2. Jiwoo: "Wow! I remember it like it was yesterday. That was my best trip ever." (와! 어제 일처럼 기억나요. 제 최고의 여행이었어요.)
3. Chloe: "Really? What was the most memorable moment?" (정말요? 가장 기억에 남는 순간은 뭐였어요?)
4. Jiwoo: "The first morning at the lake. It was the first time I’d ever been abroad. I had never seen anything like it." (호숫가에서의 첫 아침이요. 처음으로 해외에 가 본 거였어요. 그런 건 처음 봤어요.)
5. Chloe: "Aww. So what made it so special?" (아이, 좋다. 그럼 뭐가 그렇게 특별했어요?)
6. Jiwoo: "The lake was enormous, and your family was so kind. It was a once-in-a-lifetime experience." (호수가 어마어마하게 컸고, 클로이 가족이 정말 친절했어요. 평생 한 번 있을 경험이었어요.)
7. Chloe: "Once-in-a-lifetime! That sounded so natural!" (‘평생 한 번’! 정말 자연스러웠어요!)
8. Jiwoo: "Thanks! What about you? What was your most memorable project?" (고마워요! 클로이는요? 가장 기억에 남는 작업은 뭐였어요?)
9. Chloe: "My most memorable project was my first video because I made it all by myself. I put my heart and soul into it." (제일 기억에 남는 작업은 첫 영상이에요, 혼자서 다 만들었거든요. 온 마음을 다 쏟았어요.)
10. Jiwoo: "That sounds unforgettable." (잊지 못할 일이었겠네요.)
11. Chloe: "It was. Looking back, it changed my life. It still makes me smile." (그랬죠. 돌이켜 보면 그게 제 인생을 바꿨어요. 지금도 웃음이 나요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

2. Jiwoo: "Wow! I remember it like it was yesterday. That was my best trip ever." (와! 어제 일처럼 기억나요. 제 최고의 여행이었어요.)
3. Chloe: "Really? What was the most memorable moment?" (정말요? 가장 기억에 남는 순간은 뭐였어요?)
4. Jiwoo: "The first morning at the lake. It was the first time I’d ever been abroad. I had never seen anything like it." (호숫가에서의 첫 아침이요. 처음으로 해외에 가 본 거였어요. 그런 건 처음 봤어요.)
5. Chloe: "Aww. So what made it so special?" (아이, 좋다. 그럼 뭐가 그렇게 특별했어요?)
6. Jiwoo: "The lake was enormous, and your family was so kind. It was a once-in-a-lifetime experience." (호수가 어마어마하게 컸고, 클로이 가족이 정말 친절했어요. 평생 한 번 있을 경험이었어요.)
7. Chloe: "Once-in-a-lifetime! That sounded so natural!" (‘평생 한 번’! 정말 자연스러웠어요!)
8. Jiwoo: "Thanks! What about you? What was your most memorable project?" (고마워요! 클로이는요? 가장 기억에 남는 작업은 뭐였어요?)
9. Chloe: "My most memorable project was my first video because I made it all by myself. I put my heart and soul into it." (제일 기억에 남는 작업은 첫 영상이에요, 혼자서 다 만들었거든요. 온 마음을 다 쏟았어요.)
10. Jiwoo: "That sounds unforgettable." (잊지 못할 일이었겠네요.)
11. Chloe: "It was. Looking back, it changed my life. It still makes me smile." (그랬죠. 돌이켜 보면 그게 제 인생을 바꿨어요. 지금도 웃음이 나요.)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: 무엇
그건 …
왜 (because …)
rows: it was the first time I’d ever been abroad.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: What was the most memorable ___? / My most memorable ___ was ___ because ___. Table (무엇 → 그건 …):
- trip 여행 → my trip to Toronto
- day 날 → my graduation day
- party 파티 → my 30th birthday
- show 공연 → a jazz night
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
the *most* memorable trip 가장 기억에 남는 여행 
짧은 형용사는 대개 -est: big → the biggest. good은 불규칙: good → the best 
my가 있으면 the 없이: my most memorable trip
It was the first time I’d ever + p.p.

It was the first time *I’d ever been* abroad. 처음으로 해외에 가 봤어요. 
I’d = I had, 뒤에 been · seen 같은 p.p. 통째로 익혀요.
errors: the first time I’d ever see snow
the first time I’d ever seen snow
because of I saw the lake
문장 앞에는 because, 명사 앞에는 because of.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 최상급 — 가장 ~한: the most memorable trip 가장 기억에 남는 여행 / 짧은 형용사는 대개 -est: big → the biggest. good은 불규칙: good → the best / my가 있으면 the 없이: my most memorable trip
- It was the first time I’d ever + p.p.: It was the first time I’d ever been abroad. 처음으로 해외에 가 봤어요. / I’d = I had, 뒤에 been · seen 같은 p.p. 통째로 익혀요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- the most memorablest trip → the most memorable trip (most와 -est를 같이 쓰지 않아요.)
- the first time I’d ever see snow → the first time I’d ever seen snow (I’d(had) 뒤에는 p.p.)
- because of I saw the lake → because I saw the lake (문장 앞에는 because, 명사 앞에는 because of.)
- What made it so specially? → What made it so special? (make + 그것 + 형용사.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: 최상급 — 가장 ~한: the most memorable trip 가장 기억에 남는 여행 짧은 형용사는 대개 -est: big → the biggest. good은 불규칙: good → the best my가 있으면 the 없이: my most memorable trip

steps.note: 예) trip · Toronto / been abroad → My most memorable trip was my trip to Toronto. It was the first time I’d ever been abroad.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) trip · Toronto / been abroad → My most memorable trip was my trip to Toronto. It was the first time I’d ever been abroad. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: trip · Toronto → been abroad | day · my graduation → given a speech | party · my birthday → had a surprise party | show · a jazz night → heard live music.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: It was the first time I’d ever ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "What was the most memorable moment?" (가장 기억에 남는 일); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What was the most memorable ___?" / "My most memorable ___ was ___ because ___." / "It was the first time I’d ever ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I remember it like it was yesterday.
I had never seen anything like it.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 기억 떠올리기: "I’ll never forget ___." (~은 절대 못 잊을 거예요., 보통); "I remember it like it was yesterday." (어제 일처럼 기억나요., 보통); "Looking back, ___." (돌이켜 보면, ~., 보통)
- 특별했던 이유: "I had never seen anything like it." (그런 건 처음 봤어요., 보통); "It changed my life." (제 인생을 바꿨어요., 보통); "It was a once-in-a-lifetime experience." (평생 한 번 있을 경험이었어요., 보통); "It still makes me smile." (지금도 웃음이 나요., 친근)
- 맞장구치기: "What made it so special?" (뭐가 그렇게 특별했어요?, 보통); "That sounds unforgettable." (잊지 못할 일이었겠네요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: memory · memorable · unforgettable

*memory* 기억, 추억 — a happy memory 
*memorable* 기억에 남는 · *unforgettable* 잊을 수 없는(더 강함) 
*recall* 떠올리다 · my first *impression* 내 첫인상
마음을 담아 말하기

I put my *heart and soul* into it. 온 마음을 다 쏟았어요. 
It was *truly* special. 정말로 특별했어요. 
an *enormous* lake 어마어마하게 큰 호수

A: What was the ___ memorable trip?   B: Toronto. It was the first time I’d ever ___ abroad.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- memory · memorable · unforgettable: memory 기억, 추억 — a happy memory / memorable 기억에 남는 · unforgettable 잊을 수 없는(더 강함) / recall 떠올리다 · my first impression 내 첫인상
- 마음을 담아 말하기: I put my heart and soul into it. 온 마음을 다 쏟았어요. / It was truly special. 정말로 특별했어요. / an enormous lake 어마어마하게 큰 호수
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: What was the ___ memorable trip? B: Toronto. It was the first time I’d ever ___ abroad. / A: What made it so ___? B: The lake! I’ll never ___ it. / 낱말 상자: most · been · special · forget
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: memorable (기억에 남는), memory (기억, 추억), unforgettable (잊을 수 없는), impression (인상), graduation (졸업(식)), wedding (결혼식), ceremony (식, 의식), anniversary (기념일), marriage (결혼, 결혼 생활), recall (떠올리다, 기억해 내다), birth (탄생, 출생), kiss (뽀뽀, 입맞춤).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: I remember it like it was yesterday.
What was the most memorable moment?
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: lifetime (평생, 일생) — "a once-in-a-lifetime experience"; forget (잊다) — "I’ll never forget that day."; remember (기억하다) — "I remember it like it was yesterday."; moment (순간) — "What was the most memorable moment?"; experience (경험) — "It was a great experience."; special (특별한) — "What made it so special?"; change (바꾸다; 변화) — "It changed my life."; childhood (어린 시절) — "a happy childhood memory"; enormous (어마어마하게 큰) — "The lake was enormous."; truly (정말로, 진심으로) — "It was truly special.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: What was the most memorable trip or day for you?
Tell me about a ‘first time.’ What was it?

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What was the most memorable trip or day for you?" (hint on screen: My most memorable ___ was ___ because ___.)
- "Tell me about a ‘first time.’ What was it?" (hint on screen: It was the first time I’d ever ___.)
- "What’s a memory that still makes you smile?" (hint on screen: I’ll never forget ___. It still makes me smile.)
- "What was the best meal you’ve ever had?" (hint on screen: The best meal was ___.)
- "Ask me about my most memorable day." (hint on screen: What was your most memorable ___?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Chloe’s First Video
steps.text: Back in her student days, Chloe didn’t even know about the existence of jobs like ‘video designer.’ Then a small bakery near her school needed a short video. For two weeks, she *hung out* at the bakery every morning. She filmed the baker’s hands and the warm bread. On the last day, the baker *held out* a fresh cookie and said, “Show me.” At the *sight of* the video, the baker had tears in her eyes. “It was truly the best day of my life,” Chloe says. “It still *feels like* a dream.” Later, Jiwoo almost told Chloe about her application. But she didn’t. Not yet.
steps.gloss: existence 존재 · hang out 시간을 보내다 · film 촬영하다 · hold out 내밀다 · at the sight of ~을 보고 · feel like ~ 같은 느낌이 들다
questions: Where did Chloe hang out for two weeks?
What did the baker hold out?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Chloe’s First Video". Text: "Back in her student days, Chloe didn’t even know about the existence of jobs like ‘video designer.’ Then a small bakery near her school needed a short video. For two weeks, she hung out at the bakery every morning. She filmed the baker’s hands and the warm bread. On the last day, the baker held out a fresh cookie and said, “Show me.” At the sight of the video, the baker had tears in her eyes. “It was truly the best day of my life,” Chloe says. “It still feels like a dream.” Later, Jiwoo almost told Chloe about her application. But she didn’t. Not yet." Words: existence 존재 · hang out 시간을 보내다 · film 촬영하다 · hold out 내밀다 · at the sight of ~을 보고 · feel like ~ 같은 느낌이 들다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Where did Chloe hang out for two weeks?" / "What did the baker hold out?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘What was the most memorable ___?’로 가장 기억에 남는 일을 물을 수 있어요.
‘My most memorable ___ was ___ because ___.’로 이유와 함께 말할 수 있어요.
‘It was the first time I’d ever ___.’로 처음이었던 경험을 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:

- ‘My most memorable ___ was ___ because ___.’로 이유와 함께 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘It was the first time I’d ever ___.’로 처음이었던 경험을 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 그럴 걸 그랬어요
steps.title_en: I should have checked the file.
steps.goal: 작은 후회를 말하고, 바랐던 일을 말하고, 위로하기
steps.scene_desc: 3월 초 저녁, 아파트 입구 앞. 가로등 아래 지우가 휴대폰 화면(글자 없이)을 들여다보며 이마를 짚고, 장바구니를 든 벤이 다가와 걱정스러운 얼굴로 말을 거는 모습(간판·화면에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "I should have checked the file." (그럴 걸 그랬어요). Goal: 작은 후회를 말하고, 바랐던 일을 말하고, 위로하기. Today's scene: 3월 초 저녁, 아파트 입구 앞. 가로등 아래 지우가 휴대폰 화면(글자 없이)을 들여다보며 이마를 짚고, 장바구니를 든 벤이 다가와 걱정스러운 얼굴로 말을 거는 모습(간판·화면에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I should have ___.".

steps.when: 지난 일을 아쉬워해요. should have 뒤에는 *p.p.*(과거분사).
steps.extra: I should have checked the file.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I should have ___." (~했어야 했는데.). When to use it: 지난 일을 아쉬워해요. should have 뒤에는 p.p.(과거분사). Note: I should have checked the file.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I wish I had ___.".

steps.when: 지난 일이 달랐으면 하고 바라요. had 뒤에도 *p.p.*.

steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I wish I had ___." (~했더라면 좋았을 텐데.). When to use it: 지난 일이 달랐으면 하고 바라요. had 뒤에도 p.p.. Note: I wish I had asked someone to look at it.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: I should have ___. / I wish I had ___. / Don’t be too hard on yourself. Table (일어난 일 → 후회 (I should have …)):
- I was late. 늦었어요 → …left home earlier.
- I forgot her birthday. 생일을 잊었어요 → …written it down.
- I missed the bus. 버스를 놓쳤어요 → …checked the time.
- I bought the wrong size. 사이즈를 잘못 샀어요 → …tried it on.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I *should have checked* the file. 확인했어야 했는데. 
안 했어야: I *shouldn’t have sent* it so fast. 
소리로는 should’ve[슈드브]. p.p.: checked · sent · gone

I *wish I had asked* someone. 누구에게 물어봤더라면 좋았을 텐데. 
*If only I had known!* 알았더라면 좋았을걸! 
had + p.p.는 Lesson 7에서 덩어리로 본 꼴이에요.

steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- should have + p.p. — ~했어야 했는데: I should have checked the file. 확인했어야 했는데. / 안 했어야: I shouldn’t have sent it so fast. / 소리로는 should’ve[슈드브]. p.p.: checked · sent · gone
- I wish I had + p.p. — ~했더라면: I wish I had asked someone. 누구에게 물어봤더라면 좋았을 텐데. / If only I had known! 알았더라면 좋았을걸! / had + p.p.는 Lesson 7에서 덩어리로 본 꼴이에요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I should have check it. → I should have checked it. (have 뒤에는 p.p.)
- I should had checked it. → I should have checked it. (should 뒤에는 have.)
- I wish I have asked her. → I wish I had asked her. (지난 일은 I wish I had.)
- Don’t be too hard to yourself. → Don’t be too hard on yourself. (‘~에게 엄하게’는 hard on.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "I should have checked the file." (그럴 걸 그랬어요); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I should have ___." / "I wish I had ___." / "Don’t be too hard on yourself.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 후회 말하기: "I shouldn’t have said that." (그 말은 하지 말았어야 했어요., 보통); "I regret not ___ing." (~하지 않은 게 후회돼요., 보통); "If only I had known." (알았더라면 좋았을걸., 보통); "It’s too late now." (이제는 너무 늦었어요., 보통)
- 위로하기: "Everyone makes mistakes." (누구나 실수해요., 보통); "You did your best." (최선을 다했잖아요., 보통); "It’s not the end of the world." (세상이 끝난 건 아니에요., 친근)
- 앞을 보기: "Learn from it." (그걸로 배우면 돼요., 보통); "Look on the bright side." (좋은 쪽을 봐요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.

steps.teach:

What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: What’s a small mistake you made recently?
Is there a hobby you wish you had started earlier?
I wish I had started ___ earlier.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What’s a small mistake you made recently?" (hint on screen: I ___. I should have ___.)
- "Is there a hobby you wish you had started earlier?" (hint on screen: I wish I had started ___ earlier.)
- "Your friend sent the wrong file. What do you say?" (hint on screen: Don’t be too hard on yourself. Everyone makes mistakes.)
- "What did you learn from a small mistake?" (hint on screen: Now I always ___.)
- "Ask me about a small regret." (hint on screen: Is there anything you should have done differently?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: A Second Chance
steps.text: That night, Jiwoo fixed her portfolio file. This time, she asked Ben to look at it before sending it. Then she wrote a short email to Maya: “I’m afraid I attached the wrong file. Would it be possible to send you the new one?” She couldn’t *afford to* be careless again, so she read it three times. Surely it was fine. Still, she felt a little guilty. The next morning, Maya replied: “No problem! We’re merely in the first phase of hiring. Just send it to the same address.” Jiwoo felt so relieved. Ben sent her a message, too: “*Above all*, learn from it. Your hard work will *pay off*.”

questions: Who looked at the new file?
What did Ben say in his message?

steps.title: 정중하게 부탁하기
steps.title_en: Would you mind practicing with me?
steps.goal: Would you mind로 부탁하고, 괜찮다고 답하고, 더 정중하게 부탁하기
steps.scene_desc: 3월 평일 저녁, 아파트 5층 복도. 퇴근한 지우가 가방을 멘 채 휴대폰을 들고 들뜬 얼굴로 이야기하고, 옆집 그레이스가 현관문을 반쯤 연 채 두 손을 모으며 반갑게 웃음(글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Would you mind practicing with me?" (정중하게 부탁하기). Goal: Would you mind로 부탁하고, 괜찮다고 답하고, 더 정중하게 부탁하기. Today's scene: 3월 평일 저녁, 아파트 5층 복도. 퇴근한 지우가 가방을 멘 채 휴대폰을 들고 들뜬 얼굴로 이야기하고, 옆집 그레이스가 현관문을 반쯤 연 채 두 손을 모으며 반갑게 웃음(글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Would you mind ___ing?".

steps.when: 정중하게 부탁할 때 써요. mind 뒤에는 동사 *-ing*가 와요.
steps.extra: Would you mind practicing with me?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Would you mind ___ing?" (~해 주시겠어요?). When to use it: 정중하게 부탁할 때 써요. mind 뒤에는 동사 -ing가 와요. Note: Would you mind practicing with me?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Not at all.".

steps.when: Would you mind ~?에 ‘해 줄게요’라고 답할 때 써요. 직역은 ‘전혀 싫지 않아요’.
steps.extra: A: Would you mind waiting? B: Not at all.
steps.teach:

Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I’d appreciate it if you could ___.".

steps.en: I’d appreciate it if you could ___.
steps.when: 아주 정중하게 부탁할 때 써요. could 뒤에는 동사원형.

9. Jiwoo: "Deal! I really appreciate it, Grace." (좋아요! 정말 고마워요, 그레이스.)
10. Grace: "Don’t mention it. That’s what neighbors are for." (별말씀을요. 이웃 좋다는 게 뭐예요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

6. Grace: "Sure. Let’s do it step by step. First, write your questions on index cards." (그래요. 차근차근 해 봐요. 먼저 질문을 메모 카드에 적어 와요.)
7. Jiwoo: "Good idea. Do you mind if I record our practice? I want to check my answers later." (좋은 생각이에요. 연습하는 걸 녹음해도 괜찮을까요? 나중에 제 대답을 확인하고 싶어요.)
8. Grace: "Go ahead. But let’s practice at my place, not here in the hallway!" (그러세요. 그런데 여기 복도 말고 우리 집에서 연습해요!)
9. Jiwoo: "Deal! I really appreciate it, Grace." (좋아요! 정말 고마워요, 그레이스.)
10. Grace: "Don’t mention it. That’s what neighbors are for." (별말씀을요. 이웃 좋다는 게 뭐예요.)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: 부탁할 일
Would you mind ~ing?
답하기
rows: Would you mind *turning down* the music?
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Would you mind ___ing? / Not at all. / No problem. Table (부탁할 일 → Would you mind ~ing?):
- 창문 열기 → Would you mind opening the window?
- 내 대답 봐 주기 → Would you mind checking my answers?
- 음악 소리 줄이기 → Would you mind turning down the music?
- 잠깐 기다리기 → Would you mind waiting a minute?
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
mind 뒤에는 *-ing*: Would you mind *practicing* with me? 
mind는 ‘꺼리다’라서 들어줄 때는 ‘안 싫어요’ 쪽으로: Not at all. · No problem.
Do you mind if I ~? · I’d appreciate it if you could ~.

허락 구하기: Do you mind if I *record* this? → Go ahead. 
더 정중하게: I’d appreciate it if you *could ask* me. (could + 동사원형)
errors: Would you mind to help me?
I’d appreciate if you could help.
I’d appreciate it if you could help.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- Would you mind + 동사-ing?: mind 뒤에는 -ing: Would you mind practicing with me? / mind는 ‘꺼리다’라서 들어줄 때는 ‘안 싫어요’ 쪽으로: Not at all. · No problem.
- Do you mind if I ~? · I’d appreciate it if you could ~.: 허락 구하기: Do you mind if I record this? → Go ahead. / 더 정중하게: I’d appreciate it if you could ask me. (could + 동사원형)
Common mistakes on screen:
- Would you mind to help me? → Would you mind helping me? (mind 뒤에는 to 대신 -ing.)
- I’d appreciate if you could help. → I’d appreciate it if you could help. (appreciate 뒤의 it을 빼지 않아요.)
- Don’t mention about it. → Don’t mention it. (‘별말씀을요’는 about 없이 Don’t mention it.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: Would you mind + 동사-ing?: mind 뒤에는 -ing: Would you mind practicing with me? mind는 ‘꺼리다’라서 들어줄 때는 ‘안 싫어요’ 쪽으로: Not at all. · No problem.
Do you mind if I ~? · I’d appreciate it if you could ~.: 허락 구하기: Do you mind if I record this? → Go ahead. 더 정중하게: I’d appreciate it if you could ask me. (could + 동사원형)

I’d appreciate if you could help. → I’d appreciate it if you could help.

steps.note: 예) practice with me → Would you mind practicing with me? — Not at all.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) practice with me → Would you mind practicing with me? — Not at all. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: practice with me → 같이 연습하기 | check my portfolio → 포트폴리오 봐 주기 | ask me hard questions → 어려운 질문 해 주기 | speak a little slower → 조금 천천히 말하기.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: I’d appreciate it if you could ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Would you mind practicing with me?" (정중하게 부탁하기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Would you mind ___ing?" / "Not at all." / "I’d appreciate it if you could ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I was wondering if you could ___.
It would be a big help.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 부탁하기: "Sorry to bother you, but ___." (귀찮게 해서 미안하지만 ~., 정중); "Could I possibly ___?" (혹시 제가 ~해도 될까요?, 정중); "I was wondering if you could ___." (~해 주실 수 있을까 해서요., 정중)
- 허락 구하고 답하기: "Do you mind if I ___?" (제가 ~해도 괜찮을까요?, 보통); "Go ahead." (그러세요., 보통); "Actually, I’d rather you didn’t." (사실은 안 그러셨으면 해요., 정중)
- 고마움 주고받기: "It would be a big help." (큰 도움이 될 거예요., 보통); "I really appreciate it." (정말 고마워요., 보통); "Don’t mention it." (별말씀을요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: mind로 물으면 답은 거꾸로

Would you mind …? = ‘~하는 게 싫으세요?’ 
해 줄 때: Not at all. · No problem. · Of course not. 
안 될 때: Sorry, I can’t right now. · (Do you mind if I …?에) Actually, I’d rather you didn’t. 
일상에서는 Sure!(해 줄게요)도 자주 들려요.
참고 · 덩어리 표현

*I would say* you’re ready. 제 생각엔 준비된 것 같아요(부드러운 의견) 
I *could hardly* speak. 거의 말을 못 했어요 
*throw out* old cards 오래된 카드를 버리다 
Let’s not push *ourselves*. 우리 너무 무리하지 말아요
steps.blank:
A: Would you ___ practicing with me?   B: Not at ___. When? 
A: Saturday? I’d ___ it if you could ask hard questions. 
B: Sure!   A: Thanks. I really appreciate it.   B: Don’t ___ it. 
낱말 상자: mind · all · appreciate · mention
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- mind로 물으면 답은 거꾸로: Would you mind …? = ‘~하는 게 싫으세요?’ / 해 줄 때: Not at all. · No problem. · Of course not. / 안 될 때: Sorry, I can’t right now. · (Do you mind if I …?에) Actually, I’d rather you didn’t. / 일상에서는 Sure!(해 줄게요)도 자주 들려요.
- 참고 · 덩어리 표현: I would say you’re ready. 제 생각엔 준비된 것 같아요(부드러운 의견) / I could hardly speak. 거의 말을 못 했어요 / throw out old cards 오래된 카드를 버리다 / Let’s not push ourselves. 우리 너무 무리하지 말아요
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Would you ___ practicing with me? B: Not at ___. When? / A: Saturday? I’d ___ it if you could ask hard questions. / B: Sure! A: Thanks. I really appreciate it. B: Don’t ___ it. / 낱말 상자: mind · all · appreciate · mention
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: request (부탁, 요청), permission (허락), polite (공손한, 예의 바른), grateful (고마워하는), accompany (함께 가다, 동행하다), disturb (방해하다), favor (부탁, 호의), help (돕다; 도움), allow (허락하다, 허용하다), kind (친절한), trouble (수고, 번거로움). Review words: bother (귀찮게 하다).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: Could I possibly borrow your pen?
I was wondering if you could help me.
She asked in a polite manner.
I wrote each question on an index card.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: appreciate (고맙게 여기다) — "I really appreciate it."; possibly ((부탁할 때) 혹시) — "Could I possibly borrow your pen?"; wonder (궁금하다) — "I was wondering if you could help me."; manner (방식, 태도) — "She asked in a polite manner."; mind (꺼리다, 싫어하다(앞에서는 ‘마음, 생각’)) — "Would you mind waiting?"; actually (사실은) — "Actually, I’d rather you didn’t."; rather ((I’d rather) 차라리 ~하겠다) — "I’d rather stay home tonight."; index card (메모 카드(작은 카드)) — "I wrote each question on an index card."; observation (관찰; 보고 알게 된 점) — "Here’s one observation."; elsewhere (다른 곳에서) — "Let’s practice elsewhere next time.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Would you mind telling me about your weekend?
Not at all. Last weekend, I ___.
You need help with something small. Ask me politely.
Would you mind ___ing? / I was wondering if you could ___.

Go ahead. / Actually, I’d rather you didn’t. It’s a bit cold.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Would you mind telling me about your weekend?" (hint on screen: Not at all. Last weekend, I ___.)
- "You need help with something small. Ask me politely." (hint on screen: Would you mind ___ing? / I was wondering if you could ___.)
- "Do you mind if I open the window?" (hint on screen: Go ahead. / Actually, I’d rather you didn’t. It’s a bit cold.)
- "Is it easy for you to ask for help? Why or why not?" (hint on screen: Yes, because ___. / Not really. I ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Practice at Grace’s
steps.text: On Saturday, Jiwoo knocked on Grace’s door with a stack of index cards. Each card had one interview question on it. They sat at the kitchen table, and Grace asked the questions one by one. At first, Jiwoo *could hardly* speak. Her hands were cold, and her answers were too short. “We don’t have to do everything today,” Grace said. “Let’s not push ourselves.” After an hour, Grace shared one observation: “You look down at your cards too much. Look at me instead.” Jiwoo tried again and again. In the end, she decided to *throw out* half of the cards. She didn’t need them anymore. “*I would say* you’re almost ready,” Grace smiled. “Next time, let’s practice elsewhere, maybe at a café. It’ll feel more real.”
steps.gloss: index card 메모 카드 · could hardly 거의 ~할 수 없었다 · push ourselves 무리하다 · observation 보고 알게 된 점 · throw out 버리다 · I would say 제 생각엔 ~ 같아요 · elsewhere 다른 곳에서
questions: What did Jiwoo write on the index cards?
What was Grace’s observation?

Reading on screen: "Practice at Grace’s". Text: "On Saturday, Jiwoo knocked on Grace’s door with a stack of index cards. Each card had one interview question on it. Look at me instead.” Jiwoo tried again and again. In the end, she decided to throw out half of the cards. She didn’t need them anymore. “I would say you’re almost ready,” Grace smiled. “Next time, let’s practice elsewhere, maybe at a café. It’ll feel more real.”" Words: index card 메모 카드 · could hardly 거의 ~할 수 없었다 · push ourselves 무리하다 · observation 보고 알게 된 점 · throw out 버리다 · I would say 제 생각엔 ~ 같아요 · elsewhere 다른 곳에서.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Jiwoo write on the index cards?" / "What was Grace’s observation?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘Would you mind ___ing?’로 정중하게 부탁하고, ‘Not at all.’로 들어줄 수 있어요.
‘Do you mind if I ___?’로 허락을 구하고, ‘Go ahead.’로 답할 수 있어요.
‘I’d appreciate it if you could ___.’로 더 정중하게 부탁하고 고마움을 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘Would you mind ___ing?’로 정중하게 부탁하고, ‘Not at all.’로 들어줄 수 있어요.
- ‘Do you mind if I ___?’로 허락을 구하고, ‘Go ahead.’로 답할 수 있어요.

Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 소식 전하기
steps.title_en: Did you hear about the bakery?
steps.goal: 소식을 꺼내고, 들은 것을 전하고, ‘듣자 하니’로 덧붙이기
steps.scene_desc: 3월 토요일 오전, 동네 공원 산책로. 운동복 차림의 벤이 공원 건너편 모퉁이 빵집 쪽을 손으로 가리키며 이야기하고, 텀블러를 든 지우가 놀란 얼굴로 들음. 나무에 새싹이 막 돋음(간판·글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Did you hear about the bakery?" (소식 전하기). Goal: 소식을 꺼내고, 들은 것을 전하고, ‘듣자 하니’로 덧붙이기. Today's scene: 3월 토요일 오전, 동네 공원 산책로. 운동복 차림의 벤이 공원 건너편 모퉁이 빵집 쪽을 손으로 가리키며 이야기하고, 텀블러를 든 지우가 놀란 얼굴로 들음. 나무에 새싹이 막 돋음(간판·글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Did you hear about ___?".

steps.when: 새 소식을 꺼낼 때 써요. about 뒤에는 명사가 와요.
steps.extra: Did you hear about the bakery?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Did you hear about ___?" (~ 소식 들었어요?). When to use it: 새 소식을 꺼낼 때 써요. about 뒤에는 명사가 와요. Note: Did you hear about the bakery?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I heard (that) ___.".

steps.when: 남에게 들은 소식을 전할 때 써요. that은 빼도 돼요.
steps.extra: I heard it’s getting a remodel.
steps.teach:

Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "Apparently, ___.".

steps.when: 직접 확인한 건 아니고, 들은 내용을 덧붙일 때 써요.
steps.extra: Apparently, it’ll reopen in April.

Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Did you hear about ___? / I heard (that) ___. Apparently, ___. Table (Did you hear about …? → I heard (that) …):
- the bakery → I heard it’s getting a remodel.
- the park → I heard there’s a new court.
- the weather → I heard it’s going to snow.
- the subway → I heard it’s running late.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
들은 소식: I heard (that) it’s *closing*. that은 빼도 돼요. 
*Apparently*, it’ll reopen soon. 듣자 하니(직접 확인한 건 아님)

소식을 물을 때: Did you *hear about* the bakery? 
들어 본 적이 있는지: Have you *heard of* pickleball?
errors: Apparently 뒤에는 that 없이 바로 문장.
post가 아니라 posted. Keep me posted(소식 계속 알려 줘요).
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- I heard (that) + 문장 · Apparently, + 문장: 들은 소식: I heard (that) it’s closing. that은 빼도 돼요. / Apparently, it’ll reopen soon. 듣자 하니(직접 확인한 건 아님)
- hear about · heard of: 소식을 물을 때: Did you hear about the bakery? / 들어 본 적이 있는지: Have you heard of pickleball?
Common mistakes on screen:
- I listened that it’s closing. → I heard that it’s closing. (소식을 ‘들었다’는 heard. listen은 ‘귀 기울여 듣다’.)
- Apparently, that it’s closing. → Apparently, it’s closing. (Apparently 뒤에는 that 없이 바로 문장.)
- Keep me post. → Keep me posted. (post가 아니라 posted. Keep me posted(소식 계속 알려 줘요).)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) the bakery / getting a remodel → Did you hear about the bakery? I heard it’s getting a remodel.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) the bakery / getting a remodel → Did you hear about the bakery? I heard it’s getting a remodel. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: the bakery → getting a remodel | the park → getting a new court | the library → open late now | the weather → going to snow.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "Did you hear about the bakery?" (소식 전하기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Did you hear about ___?" / "I heard (that) ___." / "Apparently, ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I’m not sure if it’s true.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 소식 꺼내기: "Have you heard the news?" (그 소식 들었어요?, 보통); "Word is that ___." (~라는 말이 있어요., 친근); "It’s all over the news." (뉴스에 온통 그 얘기예요., 보통)

Picture words on screen. New: rumor (소문), gossip (남 이야기, 뒷말), newspaper (신문), announce (발표하다, 알리다), secret (비밀), spread (퍼지다, 퍼뜨리다), event (행사), court ((농구·테니스 등의) 코트), source ((소식의) 출처), news (소식, 뉴스), report (보도하다; 보도). Review words: update (새 소식, 업데이트).

items: Did you hear the recent news?
I’m not sure if it’s true.

steps.teach:
Word list on screen: apparently (듣자 하니, 보아하니) — "Apparently, it’ll reopen in April."; serious (진지한, 진심인) — "Are you serious?"; recent (최근의) — "Did you hear the recent news?"; true (사실인) — "I’m not sure if it’s true."; latest (최신의) — "What’s the latest news?"; word (말, 소문(Word is that ~)) — "Word is that it’s getting a court."; widely (널리) — "The news spread widely."; largely (대체로, 주로) — "The rumor was largely true."; association (협회, (주민) 모임) — "the neighborhood association"; notion ((막연한) 생각) — "I had a notion that it was just gossip.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.

items: Did you hear any good news this week?
Tell me some news about your favorite café or shop.
Where do you usually get your news?

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Did you hear any good news this week?" (hint on screen: Yes! I heard (that) ___. / Not really.)
- "Tell me some news about your favorite café or shop." (hint on screen: Did you hear about ___? Apparently, ___.)
- "Where do you usually get your news?" (hint on screen: I usually read ___. / I watch ___.)
- "A friend tells you a surprising rumor. What do you say?" (hint on screen: Are you serious? Where did you hear that?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Ben’s Rumor Check
steps.text: On Sunday morning, Ben *pulled back* the curtains and looked down at the park. Was the court rumor true? By then, the story was all over the building. It spread widely, but some neighbors had a notion that it was just gossip. Ben wanted a good source, so he went to the neighborhood association meeting. There, the leader announced the plan. The rumor was largely true. The park is getting a new court, but it’s for pickleball, not basketball! “Has anyone *heard of* pickleball?” she asked. Only two people raised their hands. “It’s like small tennis,” she explained. “And we’re *short of* volunteers for the opening event.” Ben raised his hand. Then he texted Jiwoo, “Update: it’s pickleball!”

steps.scene_desc: 3월 중순 평일 점심, 회사 옥상 쉼터. 바람에 머리카락이 살짝 날리고, 외투를 입은 지우와 클로이가 벤치에 나란히 앉아 있음. 클로이가 쿠키 하나를 지우에게 내밀며 웃고, 지우가 쑥스럽게 웃으며 받음. 옆에 접이식 의자 몇 개(글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "I think I owe you an apology." (친구와 다퉜어요). Goal: 다툰 일을 말하고 화해하자고 하기. Today's scene: 3월 중순 평일 점심, 회사 옥상 쉼터. 바람에 머리카락이 살짝 날리고, 외투를 입은 지우와 클로이가 벤치에 나란히 앉아 있음. 클로이가 쿠키 하나를 지우에게 내밀며 웃고, 지우가 쑥스럽게 웃으며 받음. 옆에 접이식 의자 몇 개(글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "We had an argument.".

steps.teach:

Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I think I owe her an apology.".

steps.title: On the Rooftop · 3월 중순 점심, 회사 옥상 쉼터에서

lines.en: Chloe, can we talk about what happened this morning?
lines.ko: 클로이, 오늘 아침 일에 대해 얘기 좀 할 수 있을까요?

lines.en: Sure. Sorry, I think I overreacted. But I was really hurt.
lines.ko: 그래요. 미안해요, 내가 너무 과하게 반응한 것 같아요. 그래도 정말 서운했어요.

lines.en: I know. You heard about my application from Maya, not from me.
lines.ko: 알아요. 내 지원 소식을 나한테서가 아니라 마야한테서 들었죠.

lines.en: Yes! She thought I already knew. Why didn’t you tell me?
lines.ko: 맞아요! 마야는 내가 이미 아는 줄 알았대요. 왜 말 안 했어요?

lines.en: I didn’t mean to hurt you. I felt bad about leaving our team, so I waited. I should have told you first.
lines.ko: 상처 주려던 건 아니었어요. 우리 팀을 떠나는 게 마음에 걸려서 미뤘어요. 클로이한테 먼저 말했어야 했는데.

lines.en: I see. I just felt a little ignored. I thought you didn’t trust me.
lines.ko: 그렇구나. 그냥 좀 무시당한 기분이었어요. 나를 안 믿는 줄 알았어요.

lines.en: Of course I trust you! {{I think I owe you an apology.}} I’m really sorry, Chloe.
lines.ko: 당연히 믿죠! 내가 사과해야 할 것 같아요. 정말 미안해요, 클로이.

lines.en: I accept your apology. And I’m sorry I was so cold. It was just a misunderstanding.
lines.ko: 사과 받을게요. 나도 쌀쌀맞게 굴어서 미안해요. 그냥 오해였어요.

lines.en: So… {{let’s make up}}? Let’s put it behind us.
lines.ko: 그럼… 우리 화해해요? 지난 일은 잊어요.

lines.en: Ooh, “put it behind us.” That sounded so natural! Friends again?
lines.ko: 오, ‘put it behind us’. 정말 자연스러웠어요! 다시 친구죠?

lines.en: Friends again! From now on, you’ll hear my news first.
lines.ko: 다시 친구죠! 이제부터 내 소식은 클로이가 제일 먼저 들을 거예요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "On the Rooftop · 3월 중순 점심, 회사 옥상 쉼터에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Jiwoo: "Chloe, can we talk about what happened this morning?" (클로이, 오늘 아침 일에 대해 얘기 좀 할 수 있을까요?)
2. Chloe: "Sure. Sorry, I think I overreacted. But I was really hurt." (그래요. 미안해요, 내가 너무 과하게 반응한 것 같아요. 그래도 정말 서운했어요.)
3. Jiwoo: "I know. You heard about my application from Maya, not from me." (알아요. 내 지원 소식을 나한테서가 아니라 마야한테서 들었죠.)
4. Chloe: "Yes! She thought I already knew. Why didn’t you tell me?" (맞아요! 마야는 내가 이미 아는 줄 알았대요. 왜 말 안 했어요?)
5. Jiwoo: "I didn’t mean to hurt you. I felt bad about leaving our team, so I waited. I should have told you first." (상처 주려던 건 아니었어요. 우리 팀을 떠나는 게 마음에 걸려서 미뤘어요. 클로이한테 먼저 말했어야 했는데.)
6. Chloe: "I see. I just felt a little ignored. I thought you didn’t trust me." (그렇구나. 그냥 좀 무시당한 기분이었어요. 나를 안 믿는 줄 알았어요.)
7. Jiwoo: "Of course I trust you! I think I owe you an apology. I’m really sorry, Chloe." (당연히 믿죠! 내가 사과해야 할 것 같아요. 정말 미안해요, 클로이.)
8. Chloe: "I accept your apology. And I’m sorry I was so cold. It was just a misunderstanding." (사과 받을게요. 나도 쌀쌀맞게 굴어서 미안해요. 그냥 오해였어요.)
9. Jiwoo: "So… let’s make up? Let’s put it behind us." (그럼… 우리 화해해요? 지난 일은 잊어요.)
10. Chloe: "Ooh, “put it behind us.” That sounded so natural! Friends again?" (오, ‘put it behind us’. 정말 자연스러웠어요! 다시 친구죠?)
11. Jiwoo: "Friends again! From now on, you’ll hear my news first." (다시 친구죠! 이제부터 내 소식은 클로이가 제일 먼저 들을 거예요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.
