11. Jiwoo: "Friends again! From now on, you’ll hear my news first." (다시 친구죠! 이제부터 내 소식은 클로이가 제일 먼저 들을 거예요.)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: I think I owe you an apology. I didn’t mean to ___.
head: We had a fight about …
사과하기
받아 주기
rows: I didn’t mean to hurt you.
I think I owe you an apology.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: I think I owe you an apology. I didn’t mean to ___. / Let’s make up. Friends again? Table (We had a fight about … → 사과하기):
- the trip → I didn’t mean to hurt you.
- the plan → I overreacted. I’m sorry.
- the dishes → I think I owe you an apology.
- the TV → It was just a misunderstanding.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I *owe* you *an apology*. 너한테 사과할 게 있어요(사과를 빚졌어요). 
I think I owe *her* an apology. · 비슷한 말: I owe you one. 신세 졌어요

Let’s *make up*. 화해하자 · 과거: We *made up*. 
누구와: I made up *with* Chloe. (make up a story는 ‘지어내다’)
errors: I didn’t mean to hurt you.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- owe + 사람 + an apology: I owe you an apology. 너한테 사과할 게 있어요(사과를 빚졌어요). / I think I owe her an apology. · 비슷한 말: I owe you one. 신세 졌어요
- make up 화해하다: Let’s make up. 화해하자 · 과거: We made up. / 누구와: I made up with Chloe. (make up a story는 ‘지어내다’)
Common mistakes on screen:
- I owe you an apologize. → I owe you an apology. (apology는 명사(사과), apologize는 동사(사과하다).)
- We had an argue. → We had an argument. (argue는 동사, ‘말다툼’은 argument.)
- I didn’t mean hurt you. → I didn’t mean to hurt you. (‘~하려던 건 아니에요’는 mean to + 동사원형.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: owe + 사람 + an apology: I owe you an apology. 너한테 사과할 게 있어요(사과를 빚졌어요). I think I owe her an apology. · 비슷한 말: I owe you one. 신세 졌어요
make up 화해하다: Let’s make up. 화해하자 · 과거: We made up. 누구와: I made up with Chloe. (make up a story는 ‘지어내다’)
mistakes: I owe you an apologize. → I owe you an apology.
We had an argue. → We had an argument.
I didn’t mean hurt you. → I didn’t mean to hurt you.

steps.note: 예) the trip / I overreacted. → We had a fight about the trip. I think I owe you an apology. I overreacted.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) the trip / I overreacted. → We had a fight about the trip. I think I owe you an apology. I overreacted. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: the trip → I overreacted. | the plan → I didn’t listen. | the dishes → It was my fault. | the TV → I should have asked.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: I think I owe her an apology.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "I think I owe you an apology." (친구와 다퉜어요); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "We had an argument." / "I think I owe her an apology." / "Let’s make up.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I didn’t mean to hurt you.
Can we talk about what happened?
있었던 일에 대해 얘기할 수 있을까요?
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 다툰 일 말하기: "We had a fight about ___." (~ 때문에 싸웠어요., 보통); "It was just a misunderstanding." (그냥 오해였어요., 보통); "I overreacted." (내가 과민 반응했어요., 보통)
- 사과하기: "I didn’t mean to hurt you." (상처 주려던 건 아니었어요., 보통); "Can we talk about what happened?" (있었던 일에 대해 얘기할 수 있을까요?, 정중)
- 받아 주고 화해하기: "I accept your apology." (사과 받을게요., 정중); "Let’s put it behind us." (지난 일은 잊어요., 보통); "I’m glad we talked." (얘기해서 다행이에요., 보통); "Friends again?" (다시 친구지?, 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: argument · fight · conflict

an *argument* 말다툼 · a *fight* 싸움(말싸움도 fight라고 해요) 
a *conflict* 갈등(일터·글에서 자주 써요) 
Don’t *accuse* me! 나를 탓하지 마요.
참고 · 덩어리 표현

*bring up* a topic 이야기를 꺼내다 · *bring out* cookies 과자를 꺼내 오다 
*put on* a jacket 입다 · *put back* the chairs 의자를 제자리에 두다 
(참고) *abuse* 남용하다: Don’t abuse the ‘reply all’ button.
steps.blank:
A: Can we talk about what ___?   B: Sure. 
A: I didn’t ___ to hurt you. I think I owe you an ___.

낱말 상자: happened · mean · apology · accept
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- argument · fight · conflict: an argument 말다툼 · a fight 싸움(말싸움도 fight라고 해요) / a conflict 갈등(일터·글에서 자주 써요) / Don’t accuse me! 나를 탓하지 마요.
- 참고 · 덩어리 표현: bring up a topic 이야기를 꺼내다 · bring out cookies 과자를 꺼내 오다 / put on a jacket 입다 · put back the chairs 의자를 제자리에 두다 / (참고) abuse 남용하다: Don’t abuse the ‘reply all’ button.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Can we talk about what ___? B: Sure. / A: I didn’t ___ to hurt you. I think I owe you an ___. / B: I ___ your apology. Let’s make up. A: Friends again? / 낱말 상자: happened · mean · apology · accept
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: argument (말다툼), fight (싸움; 싸우다), apology (사과), shout (소리치다), anger (화, 분노), ignore (무시하다), forgive (용서하다), friendship (우정), conflict (갈등), accuse ((잘못했다고) 탓하다, 비난하다). Review words: apologize (사과하다), calm (차분한; 진정하다).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: I didn’t mean to hurt you.
뒤에(put it behind us 지난 일로 하다)
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: misunderstanding (오해) — "It was just a misunderstanding."; overreact (과민 반응하다) — "I overreacted. I’m sorry."; glad (기쁜, 다행인) — "I’m glad we talked."; intention (의도) — "My intention was good."; hurt ((마음을) 아프게 하다) — "I didn’t mean to hurt you."; mean (~할 생각이다, 의도하다) — "I didn’t mean to."; accept (받아들이다) — "I accept your apology."; behind (뒤에(put it behind us 지난 일로 하다)) — "Let’s put it behind us."; trust (믿다; 믿음) — "Of course I trust you!"; moral support (마음으로 하는 응원) — "Thanks for the moral support.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Imagine you had a fight with a friend about a trip. How do you start the talk?
Can we talk about what happened? I think I owe you an apology.
Your friend says, “I’m sorry. I overreacted.” What do you say?
I accept your apology. / Let’s put it behind us.
Is it easy for you to say sorry first? Why or why not?
I think ___ is important in a friendship.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Imagine you had a fight with a friend about a trip. How do you start the talk?" (hint on screen: Can we talk about what happened? I think I owe you an apology.)
- "Your friend says, “I’m sorry. I overreacted.” What do you say?" (hint on screen: I accept your apology. / Let’s put it behind us.)
- "Is it easy for you to say sorry first? Why or why not?" (hint on screen: Yes, because ___. / Not really. I ___.)
- "What makes a good friendship?" (hint on screen: I think ___ is important in a friendship.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Jiwoo’s Journal
steps.text: Today Chloe and I had an argument. This morning, she *brought up* my application at the coffee machine. She heard about it from Maya, not from me. I just said, “It’s nothing,” and that made it worse. She looked hurt. I didn’t want to lose our friendship, so I asked her to talk at lunch. It was windy on the rooftop, so we *put on* our jackets. I explained everything and said sorry. Chloe forgave me right away. Then she *brought out* two cookies and gave me one. “For moral support,” she said. Problems can arise when friends don’t talk. *In any case*, we made up. Before we left, we *put back* the chairs and laughed. From now on, Chloe will hear my news first!
steps.gloss: bring up 이야기를 꺼내다 · (참고) nevertheless 그런데도(글에서) · put on 입다 · forgave 용서했다(forgive의 과거) · bring out 꺼내 오다 · moral support 마음으로 하는 응원 · arise 생기다 · in any case 어쨌든 · put back 제자리에 두다
questions: Where did Chloe bring up the application?
What did Chloe bring out at lunch?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Jiwoo’s Journal". Text: "Today Chloe and I had an argument. This morning, she brought up my application at the coffee machine. She heard about it from Maya, not from me. I just said, “It’s nothing,” and that made it worse. She looked hurt. I didn’t want to lose our friendship, so I asked her to talk at lunch. It was windy on the rooftop, so we put on our jackets. I explained everything and said sorry. Chloe forgave me right away. Then she brought out two cookies and gave me one. “For moral support,” she said. Problems can arise when friends don’t talk. In any case, we made up. Before we left, we put back the chairs and laughed. From now on, Chloe will hear my news first!" Words: bring up 이야기를 꺼내다 · (참고) nevertheless 그런데도(글에서) · put on 입다 · forgave 용서했다(forgive의 과거) · bring out 꺼내 오다 · moral support 마음으로 하는 응원 · arise 생기다 · in any case 어쨌든 · put back 제자리에 두다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Where did Chloe bring up the application?" / "What did Chloe bring out at lunch?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘We had an argument.’로 다툰 일을 말할 수 있어요.
‘I think I owe you an apology.’로 먼저 사과할 수 있어요.
‘Let’s make up. Friends again?’으로 화해하자고 하고, 사과를 받아 줄 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘We had an argument.’로 다툰 일을 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘I think I owe you an apology.’로 먼저 사과할 수 있어요.
- ‘Let’s make up. Friends again?’으로 화해하자고 하고, 사과를 받아 줄 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 그 사람이 그러는데
steps.title_en: She told me to bring my portfolio.
steps.goal: 다른 사람이 한 말과 부탁을 전하기
steps.scene_desc: 3월 말 평일 퇴근 무렵, 회사 앞 카페 창가 자리. 지우가 휴대폰 메모를 보며 손가락으로 하나씩 짚어 가며 이야기하고, 클로이가 라테 잔을 두 손으로 든 채 눈을 반짝이며 들음. 창밖은 해 질 녘(화면·간판에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "She told me to bring my portfolio." (그 사람이 그러는데). Goal: 다른 사람이 한 말과 부탁을 전하기. Today's scene: 3월 말 평일 퇴근 무렵, 회사 앞 카페 창가 자리. 지우가 휴대폰 메모를 보며 손가락으로 하나씩 짚어 가며 이야기하고, 클로이가 라테 잔을 두 손으로 든 채 눈을 반짝이며 들음. 창밖은 해 질 녘(화면·간판에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "She said (that) ___.".

steps.when: 다른 사람이 한 말을 전할 때 써요. 아직 사실인 일은 현재형 그대로 써도 돼요.
steps.extra: She said the interview is on April 9th.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "She said (that) ___." (그분이 ~라고 했어요.). When to use it: 다른 사람이 한 말을 전할 때 써요. 아직 사실인 일은 현재형 그대로 써도 돼요. Note: She said the interview is on April 9th.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "He told me to ___.".

steps.when: 부탁이나 안내를 전할 때 써요. told + 사람 + to + 동사원형.
steps.extra: She told me to bring my portfolio.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "He told me to ___." (그가 나한테 ~하라고 했어요.). When to use it: 부탁이나 안내를 전할 때 써요. told + 사람 + to + 동사원형. Note: She told me to bring my portfolio.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "She asked if ___.".

steps.when: 예/아니요 질문을 전할 때 써요. if 뒤에는 ‘주어 + 동사’.
steps.extra: She asked if I could do a short task.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "She asked if ___." (그분이 ~냐고 물었어요.). When to use it: 예/아니요 질문을 전할 때 써요. if 뒤에는 ‘주어 + 동사’. Note: She asked if I could do a short task.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("The Call from HR · 3월 말 퇴근 후, 회사 앞 카페에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: The Call from HR · 3월 말 퇴근 후, 회사 앞 카페에서

lines.en: So? You got a call from Maya’s company! What exactly did they say?
lines.ko: 그래서요? 마야 회사에서 전화 왔다면서요! 정확히 뭐래요?

lines.en: It was someone from HR. {{She said}} the interview is on April 9th at two.
lines.ko: 인사팀 분이었어요. 면접이 4월 9일 2시래요.

lines.en: Great! Why two o’clock?
lines.ko: 잘됐다! 왜 2시예요?

lines.en: She gave me two choices, ten or two. I chose the latter.
lines.ko: 10시랑 2시 중에 고르라고 했어요. 저는 뒤의 걸 골랐죠.

lines.en: Smart. Anything else?
lines.ko: 잘했어요. 또 다른 건요?

lines.en: Yes. {{She told me to}} bring my portfolio on a laptop. And {{she asked if}} I could do a short design task.
lines.ko: 네. 포트폴리오를 노트북에 담아 오라고 했어요. 그리고 짧은 디자인 과제를 할 수 있냐고 물었어요.

lines.en: A design task? Did she say why?
lines.ko: 디자인 과제요? 이유도 말했어요?

lines.en: She mentioned that the team wants to see how I think. She told me not to worry about speed.
lines.ko: 팀이 제가 어떻게 생각하는지 보고 싶어 한다고 했어요. 속도는 걱정하지 말라고 했고요.

lines.en: That sounds fair. Wait, you just said “She asked if I could…” That sounded so natural!
lines.ko: 공정하네요. 잠깐, 방금 ‘She asked if I could…’라고 했죠? 정말 자연스러웠어요!

lines.en: Thanks! Oh, and Maya called, too. She promised to do a mock interview with me the night before.

lines.en: Perfect. And I’ll be your number one fan!

Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.

frame: She said (that) ___. / She told me to ___.
head: 원래 한 말
전하는 말
rows: She *said* the interview is on the 9th.
She *told me to* bring my portfolio.
She *asked if* I could do a short task.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: She said (that) ___. / She told me to ___. / She asked if ___. Table (원래 한 말 → 전하는 말):
- “The interview is on the 9th.” → She said the interview is on the 9th.
- “Please bring your portfolio.” → She told me to bring my portfolio.
- “Don’t worry.” → She told me not to worry.
- “Can you do a short task?” → She asked if I could do a short task.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
She *said* (that) it’s on the 9th. said 바로 뒤에 사람(me)은 안 와요. 
부탁·안내: She *told me to* bring it. · She told me *not to* worry.

예/아니요 질문: She *asked if I could* do it. (if + 주어 + 동사) 
시제는 보통 한 칸 과거로: can → could, will → would · He said *he’d* be late.
errors: She said me to bring my portfolio.
She told me to bring my portfolio.
said 뒤에는 사람이 바로 오지 않아요. told me to로!
She asked if could I do a task.
She asked if I could do a task.
She told me not to worry.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- said · told: She said (that) it’s on the 9th. said 바로 뒤에 사람(me)은 안 와요. / 부탁·안내: She told me to bring it. · She told me not to worry.
- asked if · 시제: 예/아니요 질문: She asked if I could do it. (if + 주어 + 동사) / 시제는 보통 한 칸 과거로: can → could, will → would · He said he’d be late.
Common mistakes on screen:
- She said me to bring my portfolio. → She told me to bring my portfolio. (said 뒤에는 사람이 바로 오지 않아요. told me to로!)
- She asked if could I do a task. → She asked if I could do a task. (asked if 뒤에는 ‘주어 + 동사’ 순서.)
- She told me don’t worry. → She told me not to worry. (‘~하지 말라고’는 not to + 동사원형.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

asked if · 시제: 예/아니요 질문: She asked if I could do it. (if + 주어 + 동사) 시제는 보통 한 칸 과거로: can → could, will → would · He said he’d be late.

steps.note: 예) “Please call me back.” (Grace) → She told me to call her back.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) “Please call me back.” (Grace) → She told me to call her back. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: “I’ll be late.” (Daniel) → → said | “Please call me back.” (Grace) → → told | “Are you free on Friday?” (Ben) → → asked if | “Don’t forget the cake.” (Maya) → → told … not to.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "She told me to bring my portfolio." (그 사람이 그러는데); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "She said (that) ___." / "He told me to ___." / "She asked if ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: She told me not to worry.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 들은 말 전하기: "He said he’d be late." (늦을 거라고 했어요., 보통); "She told me not to worry." (걱정하지 말라고 했어요., 보통); "They asked me to join." (같이 하자고 했어요., 보통); "He wanted to know when ___." (언제 ~하는지 알고 싶어 했어요., 보통)
- 더 전하기: "She mentioned ___." (~ 이야기도 했어요., 보통); "He promised to ___." (~하겠다고 약속했어요., 보통)
- 되묻고 답하기: "What exactly did she say?" (정확히 뭐라고 했어요?, 보통); "Did he say why?" (이유도 말했어요?, 보통); "I’ll pass it on." (전해 줄게요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: What exactly did she ___? B: She said the interview ___ on April 9th. / She ___ me to bring my portfolio, and she ___ if I could do a short task. / A: Did she say ___? B: She mentioned the team wants to see how I think. / 낱말 상자: say · is · told · asked · why
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: whisper (속삭이다), complain (불평하다), warn (경고하다, 미리 조심하라고 하다), promise (약속하다; 약속), reply (답하다; 답장), explain (설명하다), deliver ((말·물건을) 전하다, 배달하다), admit ((잘못을) 인정하다), quote (인용하다; 인용한 말), relay ((들은 말을) 전달하다), mention (언급하다, (지나가듯) 말하다). Review words: message (메시지, 전할 말).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: She told me to bring my portfolio.
She asked if I could come.
She didn’t say a word about it.
She specifically told me to bring it.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: told (tell(말하다)의 과거) — "She told me to bring my portfolio."; said (say(말하다)의 과거) — "She said it’s on April 9th."; asked (ask(묻다, 부탁하다)의 과거) — "She asked if I could come."; exactly (정확히) — "What exactly did she say?"; paraphrase ((다른 말로) 바꿔 말하다) — "Can you paraphrase that?"; pass ((pass it on) 전하다) — "I’ll pass it on."; word (말, 한마디) — "She didn’t say a word about it."; specifically (구체적으로, 콕 집어서) — "She specifically told me to bring it."; latter ((둘 중) 뒤의 것) — "I chose the latter."; furthermore (게다가(주로 글에서)) — "Furthermore, please bring your laptop.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

steps.role: *역할 카드*의 가상 친구 민지가 전화로 한 말을 전해요: “Let’s meet at seven on Saturday.” · “Bring an umbrella.” · “Don’t be late.” · “Can you book a table?”
items: Your friend Minji called you. What did she say? (역할 카드)
What did she tell you to do? (역할 카드)
She told me to ___. / She told me not to ___.
Did she ask you anything? (역할 카드)
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Your friend Minji called you. What did she say? (역할 카드)" (hint on screen: She said (that) ___.)
- "What did she tell you to do? (역할 카드)" (hint on screen: She told me to ___. / She told me not to ___.)
- "Did she ask you anything? (역할 카드)" (hint on screen: She asked if I could ___.)
Role card on screen (the learner may answer as this role): 역할 카드의 가상 친구 민지가 전화로 한 말을 전해요: “Let’s meet at seven on Saturday.” · “Bring an umbrella.” · “Don’t be late.” · “Can you book a table?”
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: The Email from HR
steps.text: That evening, Jiwoo *switched on* her laptop and found an email from HR. It said the same things as the call. Furthermore, it explained the design task more specifically. It will take about thirty minutes, and she can use her own laptop. Jiwoo felt nervous again. Then she remembered Grace’s words. Grace told her that practice *builds up* confidence. So she opened her index cards and practiced one more time. Before bed, she texted Grace and Ben, “I *meant to* tell you earlier. The interview is on April 9th!” Ben replied first. He asked if she needed a lucky snack. Grace promised to help her practice again. Jiwoo smiled. Good neighbors make everything easier.

steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "I’d rather work in the office." (차라리 이게 좋아요). Goal: 둘 중 무엇을 하겠는지 묻고, I’d rather로 고르고, 좋은 점 말하기. Today's scene: 4월 초 평일 오후, 회사 탕비실. 클로이가 머그잔을 든 채 두 손가락을 펴 ‘둘 중 하나’를 고르라는 몸짓을 하고, 지우가 턱에 손을 대고 웃으며 고민함. 창밖에 벚꽃(글자 없이). steps.when: 둘 중 무엇을 하겠는지 물을 때 써요. Would you rather 뒤에는 동사원형.

steps.teach:

Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.

steps.when: 고른 것을 말해요. I’d rather = I would rather. than 뒤에 고르지 않은 것을 말해요.

frame: I’d rather ___ than ___. The good thing about ___ is ___.
head: 둘 중 하나
고르기 (I’d rather …)
좋은 점 말하기
rows: work at home / in the office
The good thing about it is the people.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Would you rather ___ or ___? / I’d rather ___ than ___. The good thing about ___ is ___. Table (둘 중 하나 → 고르기 (I’d rather …)):
- work at home / in the office → I’d rather work in the office.
- take a taxi / walk → I’d rather walk than take a taxi.
- eat out / cook at home → I’d rather cook at home.
- live downtown / in the suburbs → I’d rather live in the suburbs.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I*’d rather* walk. (둘 중) 차라리 걸을래요. 
I’d rather walk *than* take a taxi. 택시보다 걷는 게 나아요. 
안 하는 게 나을 때: I’d rather *not*.

I *prefer* tea to coffee. (평소) 차를 더 좋아해요. 
I*’d rather* have tea now. (이번엔) 차가 좋겠어요.

would rather 뒤에는 to 없이 동사원형.
I’d rather working in the office.
I’d rather work in the office.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- would rather + 동사원형 (than …): I’d rather walk. (둘 중) 차라리 걸을래요. / I’d rather walk than take a taxi. 택시보다 걷는 게 나아요. / 안 하는 게 나을 때: I’d rather not.
- would rather 와 prefer: I prefer tea to coffee. (평소) 차를 더 좋아해요. / I’d rather have tea now. (이번엔) 차가 좋겠어요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’d rather to work at home. → I’d rather work at home. (would rather 뒤에는 to 없이 동사원형.)
- I’d rather working in the office. → I’d rather work in the office. (~ing 대신 동사원형.)
- What do you rather do? → What would you rather do? (rather는 would와 함께 써요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: would rather + 동사원형 (than …): I’d rather walk. (둘 중) 차라리 걸을래요. I’d rather walk than take a taxi. 택시보다 걷는 게 나아요. 안 하는 게 나을 때: I’d rather not.
would rather 와 prefer: I prefer tea to coffee. (평소) 차를 더 좋아해요. I’d rather have tea now. (이번엔) 차가 좋겠어요.
mistakes: I’d rather to work at home. → I’d rather work at home.
I’d rather working in the office. → I’d rather work in the office.
What do you rather do? → What would you rather do?

steps.note: 예) work from home / work in the office → Would you rather work from home or in the office? — I’d rather work in the office.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) work from home / work in the office → Would you rather work from home or in the office? — I’d rather work in the office. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: work from home → work in the office | take a taxi → walk | eat out → cook at home | live downtown → live in the suburbs.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "I’d rather work in the office." (차라리 이게 좋아요); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Would you rather ___ or ___?" / "I’d rather ___ than ___." / "The good thing about ___ is ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 고르기 어려울 때: "That’s a hard choice." (어려운 선택이네요., 보통); "It doesn’t matter to me." (저는 상관없어요., 보통); "Either is fine." (둘 다 괜찮아요., 보통)
- 하나 고르기: "I’d go with ___." (저는 ~로 할래요., 친근); "I’d choose ___ any day." (언제든 ~를 고르죠., 친근); "It’s a no-brainer." (고민할 것도 없어요., 친근); "I’d prefer not to ___." (~는 안 하는 편이 좋겠어요., 정중)
- 좋은 점·나쁜 점 따지기: "On the one hand, ___." (한편으로는 ~., 보통); "The downside is ___." (단점은 ~예요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: upside · downside · advantage · benefit

the *upside* 좋은 면 ↔ the *downside* 나쁜 면 
a big *advantage* 큰 장점(다른 것보다 유리한 점) · a *benefit* 이득, 혜택 
*On the one hand*, … *On the other hand*, … 한편으로는 … 다른 한편으로는 …
something about · no matter · blow up

There’s *something about* the city at night. 밤 도시엔 뭔가가 있어요. 
*No matter* how small it is, … 아무리 작아도 … 
*blow up* a photo 사진을 크게 키우다(확대하다) 
a *prime* location 아주 좋은 위치
steps.blank:
A: Would you ___ work from home or in the office?   B: That’s a hard ___. I’d rather work in the office ___ at home. 
A: Why?   B: The good thing ___ the office is the people. 
낱말 상자: rather · choice · than · about
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- upside · downside · advantage · benefit: the upside 좋은 면 ↔ the downside 나쁜 면 / a big advantage 큰 장점(다른 것보다 유리한 점) · a benefit 이득, 혜택 / On the one hand, … On the other hand, … 한편으로는 … 다른 한편으로는 …
- something about · no matter · blow up: There’s something about the city at night. 밤 도시엔 뭔가가 있어요. / No matter how small it is, … 아무리 작아도 … / blow up a photo 사진을 크게 키우다(확대하다) / a prime location 아주 좋은 위치
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Would you ___ work from home or in the office? B: That’s a hard ___. I’d rather work in the office ___ at home. / A: Why? B: The good thing ___ the office is the people. / 낱말 상자: rather · choice · than · about
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: either ((둘 중) 어느 것이든), matter (중요하다, 상관있다), downside (단점, 나쁜 면), upside (장점, 좋은 면), benefit (이득, 혜택), advantage (장점, 유리한 점), trade (맞바꾸다; 거래), obvious (뻔한, 분명한), suburb (교외(도시 바깥 주택가)), downtown (시내, 도심), cozy (아늑한), spacious (넓은, 널찍한).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: I’d rather walk than take a taxi.
Working from home is a good option.
I’d choose a short commute any day.
I mainly work at my desk.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: rather ((would rather) 차라리 ~하겠다) — "I’d rather walk than take a taxi."; prefer (더 좋아하다) — "I prefer tea to coffee."; choice (선택) — "That’s a hard choice."; option (선택지) — "Working from home is a good option."; choose (고르다, 선택하다) — "I’d choose a short commute any day."; pick (고르다) — "You have to pick one!"; instead (대신에) — "Let’s walk instead."; hard (어려운) — "It’s a hard question."; mainly (주로) — "I mainly work at my desk.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Would you rather work from home or in the office? (상상해서 답해도 돼요)
Would you rather live downtown or in the suburbs?
I’d rather live ___. The good thing about it is ___.
Coffee or tea? Which would you choose any day?
I’d choose ___ any day. / Either is fine.
Ask me a “Would you rather” question.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Would you rather work from home or in the office? (상상해서 답해도 돼요)" (hint on screen: I’d rather ___ than ___.)
- "Would you rather live downtown or in the suburbs?" (hint on screen: I’d rather live ___. The good thing about it is ___.)
- "Coffee or tea? Which would you choose any day?" (hint on screen: I’d choose ___ any day. / Either is fine.)
- "Ask me a “Would you rather” question." (hint on screen: Would you rather ___ or ___?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: Would you rather work from home or in the office? (상상해서 답해도 돼요)
Would you rather live downtown or in the suburbs?
Coffee or tea? Which would you choose any day?
Ask me a “Would you rather” question.

steps.title: Chloe’s Rule
steps.text: Chloe has a rule for hard choices: answer fast, then ask why. “There’s *something about* a quick answer. It shows what you really want.” When she moved to Seoul, she had to choose between two apartments. One was tiny, but it was in a prime location downtown. The other was in the suburbs, spacious and significantly cheaper. The obvious choice was the cheap one, but Chloe picked downtown in two seconds and traded space for time. “*No matter* how small my place is, I mainly want a short commute.” She uses her rule at work, too. When a client can’t decide between cropping a photo and *blowing it up*, she asks, “Would you rather…?” It works effectively every time.
steps.gloss: prime location 아주 좋은 위치 · significantly 상당히, 크게 · obvious 뻔한 · trade A for B A를 B와 맞바꾸다 · no matter how ~ 아무리 ~해도 · blow up (사진을) 크게 키우다 · effectively 효과적으로
questions: Why did Chloe choose the tiny apartment?
What does Chloe ask a client who can’t decide?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Chloe’s Rule". Text: "Chloe has a rule for hard choices: answer fast, then ask why. “There’s something about a quick answer. It shows what you really want.” When she moved to Seoul, she had to choose between two apartments. One was tiny, but it was in a prime location downtown. The other was in the suburbs, spacious and significantly cheaper. The obvious choice was the cheap one, but Chloe picked downtown in two seconds and traded space for time. “No matter how small my place is, I mainly want a short commute.” She uses her rule at work, too. When a client can’t decide between cropping a photo and blowing it up, she asks, “Would you rather…?” It works effectively every time." Words: prime location 아주 좋은 위치 · significantly 상당히, 크게 · obvious 뻔한 · trade A for B A를 B와 맞바꾸다 · no matter how ~ 아무리 ~해도 · blow up (사진을) 크게 키우다 · effectively 효과적으로.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Why did Chloe choose the tiny apartment?" / "What does Chloe ask a client who can’t decide?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘Would you rather ___ or ___?’로 둘 중 무엇을 하겠는지 물을 수 있어요.
‘I’d rather ___ than ___.’으로 하나를 골라 말할 수 있어요.
‘The good thing about ___ is ___.’로 고른 이유와 좋은 점을 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘Would you rather ___ or ___?’로 둘 중 무엇을 하겠는지 물을 수 있어요.
- ‘I’d rather ___ than ___.’으로 하나를 골라 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘The good thing about ___ is ___.’로 고른 이유와 좋은 점을 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 면접 자기소개
steps.goal: 경력과 잘하는 것을 소개하기
steps.scene_desc: 4월 평일 저녁, 회사 근처 조용한 카페 구석 자리. 마야가 공책을 들고 면접관 흉내를 내며 일부러 진지한 표정을 짓고, 재킷을 입은 지우가 허리를 곧게 펴고 앉아 대답함. 탁자 위에 노트북과 찻잔 두 개(화면·간판에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Tell me about yourself." (면접 자기소개). Goal: 경력과 잘하는 것을 소개하기. Today's scene: 4월 평일 저녁, 회사 근처 조용한 카페 구석 자리. 마야가 공책을 들고 면접관 흉내를 내며 일부러 진지한 표정을 짓고, 재킷을 입은 지우가 허리를 곧게 펴고 앉아 대답함. 탁자 위에 노트북과 찻잔 두 개(화면·간판에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Tell me about yourself.".

steps.when: 면접에서 처음에 자주 듣는 말이에요. 일·경력 중심으로 짧게 대답해요.
steps.extra: 대답: I’m a web designer, and I love making things easy to use.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Tell me about yourself." (자기소개를 해 주세요.). When to use it: 면접에서 처음에 자주 듣는 말이에요. 일·경력 중심으로 짧게 대답해요. Note: 대답: I’m a web designer, and I love making things easy to use.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I’m good at ___ing.".

steps.when: 잘하는 것을 말해요. at 뒤에는 명사나 *동사 + ing*.
steps.extra: I’m good at solving problems. · I’m good at teamwork.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I’m good at ___ing." (~를 잘해요.). When to use it: 잘하는 것을 말해요. at 뒤에는 명사나 동사 + ing. Note: I’m good at solving problems. · I’m good at teamwork.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I’ve worked as ___ for ___ years.".

steps.when: 지금까지 이어진 경력을 말해요. 현재완료 + for + 기간.
steps.extra: I’ve worked as a web designer for six years.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I’ve worked as ___ for ___ years." (~로 ~년째 일하고 있어요.). When to use it: 지금까지 이어진 경력을 말해요. 현재완료 + for + 기간. Note: I’ve worked as a web designer for six years.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Practice Interview · 면접 전날 저녁, 회사 근처 카페에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Practice Interview · 면접 전날 저녁, 회사 근처 카페에서

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Practice Interview · 면접 전날 저녁, 회사 근처 카페에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Maya: "Remember, I’m not your interviewer, so I don’t know the real questions. Let’s just practice common ones." (기억해요, 저는 면접관이 아니라서 실제 질문은 몰라요. 흔한 질문으로만 연습해요.)

5. Maya: "Nice. What’s your biggest strength?" (좋아요. 가장 큰 강점이 뭐예요?)
6. Jiwoo: "I’m good at listen to users." (사용자 말을 듣는 걸 잘해요.)

9. Maya: "Much better. Why do you want this job?" (훨씬 좋아요. 왜 이 일을 하고 싶어요?)
10. Jiwoo: "I want to grow as a UX designer. I think I can contribute a lot to the team." (UX 디자이너로 성장하고 싶어요. 팀에 많이 기여할 수 있다고 생각해요.)
11. Maya: "You’ve got this! You’re more than capable." (할 수 있어요! 충분히 해낼 사람이에요.)
12. Jiwoo: "Thanks, Maya! And… thank you for your time." (고마워요, 마야! 그리고… (면접처럼) 시간 내 주셔서 감사합니다.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

items: Maya is one of Jiwoo’s real interviewers.
Jiwoo has worked as a web designer for six years.
Jiwoo says she works well in a team.

2. Jiwoo has worked as a web designer for six years.
3. Jiwoo says she works well in a team.
The scene they are about:

5. Maya: "Nice. What’s your biggest strength?" (좋아요. 가장 큰 강점이 뭐예요?)
6. Jiwoo: "I’m good at listen to users." (사용자 말을 듣는 걸 잘해요.)
7. Maya: "Oh, you mean “I’m good at listening to users.” Can you say that?" (아, ‘I’m good at listening to users’라는 거죠? 다시 말해 볼래요?)
8. Jiwoo: "I’m good at listening to users. And I work well in a team." (사용자 말을 듣는 걸 잘해요. 그리고 팀으로 일을 잘해요.)

11. Maya: "You’ve got this! You’re more than capable." (할 수 있어요! 충분히 해낼 사람이에요.)

Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. In Korean say the answer as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: 직업
기간 (for …)
잘하는 것 (good at …)
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: I’ve worked as ___ for ___ years. / I’m good at ___ing. Table (직업 → 기간 (for …)):
- a web designer 웹 디자이너 → for six years
- a teacher 교사 → for three years
- a nurse 간호사 → for ten years
- a cook 요리사 → for two years
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I*’ve worked* as a designer *for* six years. 6년째 일해요. 
I *worked* as a cook for two years. (예전에) 2년 일했어요.

I’m good at *design*. · I’m good at *listening*. 
My *strength* is … 강점 · One of my *weaknesses* is … 약점
errors: I’m good at listen to people.
I’m good at listening to people.
I’ve worked here since six years.
I’ve worked here for six years.
I work as a teacher for three years.
I’ve worked as a teacher for three years.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 현재완료 + for — 지금까지 이어진 경력: I’ve worked as a designer for six years. 6년째 일해요. / I worked as a cook for two years. (예전에) 2년 일했어요.
- good at + 명사 / 동사 ~ing: I’m good at design. · I’m good at listening. / My strength is … 강점 · One of my weaknesses is … 약점
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’m good at listen to people. → I’m good at listening to people. (at 뒤에는 동사 + ing.)
- I’ve worked here since six years. → I’ve worked here for six years. (기간 앞에는 for.)
- I work as a teacher for three years. → I’ve worked as a teacher for three years. (‘지금까지 ~년째’는 현재완료.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. After that, go over each remaining mistake on screen in one short sentence (the wrong one, the right one and why), so that no mistake on screen is skipped. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: 현재완료 + for — 지금까지 이어진 경력: I’ve worked as a designer for six years. 6년째 일해요. I worked as a cook for two years. (예전에) 2년 일했어요.
good at + 명사 / 동사 ~ing: I’m good at design. · I’m good at listening. My strength is … 강점 · One of my weaknesses is … 약점
mistakes: I’m good at listen to people. → I’m good at listening to people.
I’ve worked here since six years. → I’ve worked here for six years.
I work as a teacher for three years. → I’ve worked as a teacher for three years.

steps.note: 예) → I’ve worked as a web designer for six years. I’m good at solving problems.
steps.teach:
Drill. How it works (note on screen): 예) → I’ve worked as a web designer for six years. I’m good at solving problems. Items, each a pair of cues the learner uses to build the answer: designer · 6 years → solving problems | teacher · 3 years → explaining things | nurse · 10 years → staying calm | cook · 2 years → working fast.
First read the example in the note: it shows exactly what the learner says for one item and who plays which role (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes you play a role and answer). Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear and matches the example, let the learner answer, and react. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "Tell me about yourself." (면접 자기소개); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Tell me about yourself." / "I’m good at ___ing." / "I’ve worked as ___ for ___ years.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I work well in a team.
Why do you want this job?
Where do you see yourself in five years?
Do you have any questions for us?
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 나를 소개하기: "I majored in ___." (전공은 ~였어요., 보통); "My strength is ___." (제 강점은 ~예요., 정중); "One of my weaknesses is ___." (제 약점 중 하나는 ~예요., 정중); "I’m a quick learner." (저는 빨리 배워요., 보통); "I work well in a team." (팀으로 일을 잘해요., 보통)
- 면접관이 자주 묻는 말: "Why do you want this job?" (왜 이 일을 하고 싶어요?, 정중); "Where do you see yourself in five years?" (5년 뒤 어떤 모습일 것 같아요?, 정중); "Do you have any questions for us?" (저희에게 궁금한 점 있으세요?, 정중)
- 마치며: "Thank you for your time." (시간 내 주셔서 감사합니다., 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 지원할 때 쓰는 말

*apply* for a *position* 자리에 지원하다 · an *application* 지원서 
a *degree* in design 디자인 학위 · *hire* 뽑다, 고용하다 
*salary* 급여 — 언제 이야기하는지는 회사마다 달라요.
sit up · over the years · oh well

*Sit up* straight! 허리 펴고 앉아요! 
*Over the years*, I’ve learned … 그동안(여러 해에 걸쳐) … 
*Oh well*, I did my best. 뭐, 최선을 다했어요(아쉬워도 받아들일 때).
steps.blank:
A: Tell me about ___.   B: I’ve worked as a web designer ___ six years. 
A: What’s your biggest ___?   B: I’m good at ___ to users. 
낱말 상자: yourself · for · strength · listening
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 지원할 때 쓰는 말: apply for a position 자리에 지원하다 · an application 지원서 / a degree in design 디자인 학위 · hire 뽑다, 고용하다 / salary 급여 — 언제 이야기하는지는 회사마다 달라요.
- sit up · over the years · oh well: Sit up straight! 허리 펴고 앉아요! / Over the years, I’ve learned … 그동안(여러 해에 걸쳐) … / Oh well, I did my best. 뭐, 최선을 다했어요(아쉬워도 받아들일 때).
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Tell me about ___. B: I’ve worked as a web designer ___ six years. / A: What’s your biggest ___? B: I’m good at ___ to users. / 낱말 상자: yourself · for · strength · listening
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: interview (면접), team (팀), apply (지원하다), application (지원서), degree (학위), major (전공; 전공하다), position ((일)자리, 직위), salary (급여, 연봉), skill (기술, 솜씨), strength (강점, 장점), weakness (약점), achievement (이룬 일, 성과).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: I was responsible for the website.
I acquired new skills at work.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: qualified (자격을 갖춘) — "She’s qualified for the position."; responsible ((for) ~을 맡은, 책임지는) — "I was responsible for the website."; ability (능력) — "the ability to listen"; professional (전문적인; 전문가) — "a professional designer"; experience (경험, 경력) — "six years of experience"; career (경력, 커리어) — "a career in UX design"; fundamental (기본적인, 가장 중요한) — "Listening to users is fundamental."; capacity ((~할) 능력, 역량) — "the capacity to learn fast"; acquire (얻다, 익히다) — "I acquired new skills at work.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: I’ve worked as a ___ for ___ years. / I’m studying ___.
I’m good at ___ing. / My strength is ___.
One of my weaknesses is ___. But I’m practicing.
Outside of work, what are you good at?
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Tell me about yourself." (hint on screen: I’ve worked as a ___ for ___ years. / I’m studying ___.)
- "What are you good at?" (hint on screen: I’m good at ___ing. / My strength is ___.)
- "What’s one of your weaknesses?" (hint on screen: One of my weaknesses is ___. But I’m practicing.)
- "Outside of work, what are you good at?" (hint on screen: I’m good at ___ing.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: Tell me about yourself.
What are you good at?
What’s one of your weaknesses?

steps.title: Interview Day
steps.text: The next afternoon, Jiwoo met two interviewers, a design lead and an executive. Maya wasn’t there, and that was fair. Jiwoo talked about her background and her work with software engineers. She showed a brand identity project, too. “I enhanced an old logo and website,” she said. The executive looked impressed. “We employ many good designers. Why should we hire you?” Jiwoo answered calmly. On the way home, she thought, “If they reject me, *oh well*.” A week later, the phone rang. “We’d like to offer you the position.” “It’s an honor,” said Jiwoo.
steps.gloss: executive 임원 · brand identity 브랜드 이미지(로고 등) · enhance 더 좋게 하다 · employ 고용하다 · reject 떨어뜨리다 · honor 영광
questions: Who were Jiwoo’s interviewers?
What happened a week later?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Interview Day". Text: "The next afternoon, Jiwoo met two interviewers, a design lead and an executive. Maya wasn’t there, and that was fair. Jiwoo talked about her background and her work with software engineers. She showed a brand identity project, too. “I enhanced an old logo and website,” she said. The executive looked impressed. “We employ many good designers. Why should we hire you?” Jiwoo answered calmly. On the way home, she thought, “If they reject me, oh well.” A week later, the phone rang. “We’d like to offer you the position.” “It’s an honor,” said Jiwoo." Words: executive 임원 · brand identity 브랜드 이미지(로고 등) · enhance 더 좋게 하다 · employ 고용하다 · reject 떨어뜨리다 · honor 영광.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Who were Jiwoo’s interviewers?" / "What happened a week later?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘Tell me about yourself.’에 경력 중심으로 자기소개를 할 수 있어요.
‘I’ve worked as ___ for ___ years.’로 지금까지 이어진 경력을 말할 수 있어요.
‘I’m good at ___ing.’로 강점을 말하고, 면접에서 자주 묻는 질문에 답할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘Tell me about yourself.’에 경력 중심으로 자기소개를 할 수 있어요.
- ‘I’ve worked as ___ for ___ years.’로 지금까지 이어진 경력을 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘I’m good at ___ing.’로 강점을 말하고, 면접에서 자주 묻는 질문에 답할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 첫 출근
steps.goal: 새 직장에서 자신을 소개하고 도움을 구하기
steps.scene_desc: 5월 첫 월요일 아침, 밝은 새 사무실. 출입증을 목에 건 지우가 팀 동료와 악수하고, 뒤에서 마야가 노트북을 안고 웃으며 회의실 쪽으로 걸어감. 창가 책상과 화분, 복도 끝 프린터(화면·벽에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.

steps.title: Jiwoo’s First Day
steps.text: After lunch, Jiwoo, the team’s new UX designer, finished her registration and signed her employment papers. Her onboarding list included sexual harassment prevention training. Then the senior designer took her around the division, and she shook hands with everyone. The team assistant, who works *part time*, assists new staff. Later, the team had a joint meeting with marketing. Everyone was polite and civil, and together they *came up with* three new ideas. Maya smiled. “We recruit great talent,” she said. “Today, that’s you.”
steps.gloss: shake hands 악수하다 · part time 시간제로 · assist 돕다 · joint 공동의 · civil 예의 바른 · come up with 떠올리다 · recruit 뽑다 · talent 인재
questions: What did Jiwoo do after lunch?
What did the team come up with?

Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Jiwoo do after lunch?" / "What did the team come up with?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘I’m new here.’로 새 직장에서 자신을 소개할 수 있어요.
‘Could you show me around?’로 안내를 공손하게 부탁할 수 있어요.
‘Who should I ask about ___?’로 누구에게 물어야 할지 물을 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘I’m new here.’로 새 직장에서 자신을 소개할 수 있어요.
- ‘Could you show me around?’로 안내를 공손하게 부탁할 수 있어요.

Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. steps.title: 집 구하기

steps.scene_desc: 5월 주말 오후, 새 회사 근처 작은 원룸 안. 햇빛이 드는 창가를 중개인이 가리키고, 지우가 방을 둘러보며 수첩에 메모하고, 대니얼이 줄자로 벽 길이를 재며 고개를 갸웃함(벽·서류에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "How much is the rent?" (집 구하기). Goal: 집을 찾으며 조건을 묻고 계약을 상의하기. Today's scene: 5월 주말 오후, 새 회사 근처 작은 원룸 안. 햇빛이 드는 창가를 중개인이 가리키고, 지우가 방을 둘러보며 수첩에 메모하고, 대니얼이 줄자로 벽 길이를 재며 고개를 갸웃함(벽·서류에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above).
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I’m looking for a place near ___.".

steps.en: I’m looking for a place near ___.
steps.when: 집을 구할 때 원하는 곳을 말해요. look for = 찾다(찾는 중).
steps.extra: I’m looking for a place near my office.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I’m looking for a place near ___." (~ 근처 집을 찾고 있어요.). When to use it: 집을 구할 때 원하는 곳을 말해요. look for = 찾다(찾는 중). Note: I’m looking for a place near my office.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "How much is the rent?".

steps.when: 집값·요금을 물을 때 How much is ~?
steps.extra: 대답: It’s 850,000 won a month. (금액은 가상)
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "How much is the rent?" (월세가 얼마예요?). When to use it: 집값·요금을 물을 때 How much is ~? Note: 대답: It’s 850,000 won a month. (금액은 가상).
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "When can I move in?".

steps.when: 이사 들어갈 수 있는 날을 물어요. move in = 입주하다.
steps.extra: 대답: You can move in next month.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "When can I move in?" (언제 입주할 수 있어요?). When to use it: 이사 들어갈 수 있는 날을 물어요. move in = 입주하다. Note: 대답: You can move in next month.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Room Hunting · 5월 주말, 새 회사 근처 원룸에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Room Hunting · 5월 주말, 새 회사 근처 원룸에서

lines.en: So this is the place? It’s really close to your new office.
lines.ko: 여기가 그 집이에요? 새 회사랑 정말 가깝네요.

lines.en: Yes. {{I’m looking for a place near}} work.
lines.ko: 네. 회사 근처 집을 찾고 있어요.

lines.ko: 들어오세요. 원룸이고, 햇빛이 잘 들어요.

lines.en: It’s tiny, but cozy. {{How much is the rent}}?
lines.ko: 아주 작지만 아늑하네요. 월세가 얼마예요?

lines.en: It’s 850,000 won a month, with a deposit of ten million won.
lines.ko: 한 달에 85만 원이고, 보증금은 천만 원이에요.

lines.en: Is it furnished? And are utilities included?
lines.ko: 가구는 있어요? 그리고 공과금은 포함이에요?

lines.en: There’s a bed and a desk. Utilities aren’t included, but the maintenance fee is.
lines.ko: 침대랑 책상이 있어요. 공과금은 별도지만, 관리비는 포함이에요.

lines.en: I see. How long is the lease? And {{when can I move in}}?
lines.ko: 그렇군요. 계약 기간은요? 그리고 언제 입주할 수 있어요?

lines.en: It’s a one-year lease, and you can move in next month. One provision in the lease says no pets.
lines.ko: 1년 계약이고, 다음 달에 입주할 수 있어요. 계약서 조항에 반려동물은 안 된다고 돼 있어요.

lines.ko: 음. 지금 집이랑 비교해 봐요. 훨씬 작아요.

lines.en: You’re right. Thank you. I’ll think about it and call you.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 감사합니다. 생각해 보고 연락드릴게요.

Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
